previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old male with a complex medical history including kidney transplant with stage 4 CKD, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, atrial fibrillation, and prior empyema was admitted for subacute cough and mild volume overload. He had recently returned home from rehab but developed worsening chest congestion and a wet cough. Imaging revealed mild pulmonary edema, small bilateral pleural effusions, and new multifocal nodular opacities in the lungs concerning for atypical infection or inflammation. He was treated with IV diuresis for acute on chronic heart failure and monitored closely. Workup for infection, including urine and sputum cultures, showed asymptomatic bacteriuria with Citrobacter koseri, which was not treated per transplant guidelines. Infectious workup including Legionella, cryptococcal antigen, and blood cultures were negative. Given improvement in symptoms and stability, antibiotics were avoided due to risk of C. diff. Tacrolimus was adjusted downward due to elevated trough levels. He improved clinically, remained euvolemic, and was discharged home with home health services and plans for outpatient follow-up with pulmonary and infectious disease specialists to evaluate persistent radiographic findings.
